oil.summary: Crude prices posted a sharp intraday split on Wednesday: WTI shed 5.08% to $98.38/bbl while Brent fell only 0.21% to $109.32, widening the Brent-WTI spread markedly. The divergence reflects two competing forces. On the bearish side, Trump's partial waiver of Russian oil sanctions added supply-side relief, with Russia's seaborne exports already under pressure after Baltic port disruptions and Ukraine's mass drone strike on a St. Petersburg oil terminal. On the bullish side, Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities, ongoing Strait of Hormuz disruption in the US-Israel-Iran conflict, and a 4.93 million barrel US crude inventory draw reported by API all kept Brent well supported. RBOB gasoline and heating oil fell 3.86% and 3.25% respectively, suggesting demand-side softness is amplifying the WTI weakness. CME options markets price a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting.
drivers: Trump's Russia sanctions waiver pressuring WTI while Houthi strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities and Hormuz disruption underpin Brent, widening the spread
API reported a 4.93 million barrel US crude inventory draw for the week ending Oct 16, providing a partial floor
Ukraine's 1,000-drone strike on St. Petersburg oil infrastructure and halted Primorsk Baltic exports tighten Russian supply, but sanctions relief offsets the effect
sources: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

gas.summary: Natural gas prices weakened on both sides of the Atlantic on Wednesday, though the underlying supply picture remains strained. Henry Hub fell 2.52% to $2.982/MMBtu and is down 9.20% on the week, suggesting near-term US demand softness or mild weather is outweighing geopolitical support. European TTF eased 1.81% to €86.445/MWh but remains 18% higher on the month, a stark contrast reflecting tighter fundamentals. A notable bearish development for European supply came from Norway, where September natural gas output fell 12.6% month-on-month, exacerbating concerns ahead of winter. The EU simultaneously reaffirmed its opposition to Arctic gas development despite depleted storage levels. LNG market tightness linked to Middle East conflict risks was flagged in available reporting but headline detail on that front is limited.
drivers: Norway's September gas output fell 12.6% month-on-month, tightening European winter supply
EU reaffirmed opposition to Arctic gas development even as the bloc faces an expensive winter with depleted storage
Henry Hub down 9.2% on the week despite a firmer monthly trend, pointing to near-term US demand weakness overriding geopolitical support

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged up 0.89% to $81.64/EUA today, a modest recovery within a broader monthly softening of 1.08%, while TTF — the key power-sector fuel input — slipped 1.81% on the day but remains 18% higher over the past month. Structural demand signals are constructive: a separate headline noted European electricity demand has returned to growth, driven by rising electrification despite weak industrial activity. On the supply side, Mexico's state utility is set to approve up to 60 renewable energy projects totalling 8.2 GW, predominantly solar. A Nevada utility dataset showed geothermal reaching cost parity with solar-plus-storage, a meaningful milestone for firm clean power. The Strait of Hormuz situation, with Iran offering a conditional six-to-seven-day reopening window, remains a key watch point for LNG and gas-fired generation cost exposure across Europe.
drivers: European power demand returning to growth driven by electrification, supporting EUA prices despite weak industrial activity
Mexico poised to approve 8.2 GW of new renewable capacity across up to 60 projects, predominantly solar
Geothermal achieves cost parity with solar-plus-storage per Nevada utility data, while Hormuz closure risk keeps European gas-fired generation cost exposure elevated
sources: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
